newsitem.title: USA: Departing Mich. official looks to private sector.
newsitem.headline: Departing Mich. official looks to private sector.

text.p: Nick Khouri, Michigan's chief deputy treasurer, said Friday that he resigned from the position because "it was time to do something different."
That "something different" will now take Khouri to the private sector after serving six years in Michigan's treasury department and six years prior to that in the state's Senate Fiscal Agency.

He said his first job, beginning next month, will be examining the debt management and treasury operations of Guam as a consultant for Barents Group, the wholly owned government consulting subsidiary of Peat Marwick.

Starting April 1, Khouri said he would be back in Lansing, Mich., to join the staff of Public Sector Consultants. He said the job will entail advising public and private entities on a variety of financial matters.

During his six years as Michigan's chief deputy treasurer, Khouri said he was most proud of the work he did on reforming the way primary and secondary public schools were funded. The reform plan approved by voters in 1994 replaced more than $6 billion of local property taxes with a higher state sales tax and other revenues.
"It was one of the most fundamental changes in Michigan public policy ever," Khouri said, adding that while problems emerged with the new funding system, they were relatively minor.
Khouri was also reponsible for most of the state's debt issuance.
"I think we ran a clean, straightforward, relatively boring, but honest ship in the bond area," he said.

While the state was an infrequent visitor to the municipal bond market, it became entangled in the trial of former Lazard Freres & Co. partner Mark Ferber on criminal charges of fraud and conspiracy involving bond deals. Khouri was one of several government officials who testified at the Boston trial that led to Ferber's conviction.
Khouri said the episode involving Ferber, who had served as a financial adviser to the Michigan Department of Transportation, was a non-event in the state.
Also during Khouri's watch, the state enjoyed a rating upgrade from Moody's Investors Service, giving Michigan a matched set of double-A ratings from all three rating agencies.
Khouri said he did not know how Michigan Treasurer Doug Roberts planned to replace him. Roberts was not available to comment.
Khouri's departure from state government was announced by the state's treasury department on Monday.
